items.q: 다항식 P(x)를 x²−3x+2로 나눈 나머지는 2x+1이고, x−3으로 나눈 나머지는 10이다. P(x)를 (x−1)(x−2)(x−3)으로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(4)의 값은?
다항식 x²⁰²⁶+x²⁰²⁵+1을 x²+x+1로 나눈 나머지를 ax+b라 할 때, a+b의 값은?
items.x: x²+x+1=0의 근 ω는 ω³=1. ω²⁰²⁶=ω, ω²⁰²⁵=1 → 값은 ω+2. 두 근 모두에서 일치하므로 나머지는 x+2, a+b=3.

items.q: 등식 2x³−3x²+4x−1 = a(x−1)³+b(x−1)²+c(x−1)+d 가 x에 대한 항등식일 때, a+b+c+d의 값은?
items.x: x=2를 대입하면 우변은 a+b+c+d, 좌변은 16−12+8−1=11.

items.q: 실수 a, b, c가 a+b+c=0, a²+b²+c²=6을 만족할 때, a⁴+b⁴+c⁴의 값은?
items.x: ab+bc+ca=(0−6)/2=−3. a²b²+b²c²+c²a²=(ab+bc+ca)²−2abc(a+b+c)=9. a⁴+b⁴+c⁴=6²−2·9=18.

items.q: x+1/x=3일 때, x⁵+1/x⁵의 값은?
최고차항의 계수가 1인 삼차다항식 P(x)가 P(1)=2, P(2)=4, P(3)=6을 만족시킬 때, P(x)를 x−5로 나눈 나머지는?
z=(1+√3 i)/2 일 때, z²⁰²⁶ + 1/z²⁰²⁶ 의 값은?
복소수 z에 대하여 z+z̄=4, z·z̄=13일 때, z²의 허수부분의 절댓값은? (단, z̄는 z의 켤레복소수)
0이 아닌 복소수 z가 z²=z̄를 만족시킬 때, 이를 만족하는 모든 z의 곱은?
items.x: |z|²=|z| → |z|=1. 양변에 z를 곱하면 z³=zz̄=1. 따라서 z는 1, ω, ω² 이고 그 곱은 1.

items.q: 이차방정식 x²−3x+1=0의 두 근을 α, β라 할 때, (α²+α+1)(β²+β+1)의 값은?
items.x: α²=3α−1 이므로 α²+α+1=4α. 같은 방식으로 4β. 곱은 16αβ=16.

items.q: x³=1의 한 허근을 ω라 할 때, Σ(k=1~12) 1/(1+ωᵏ) 의 값은?
삼차방정식 x³−2x²+3x−4=0의 세 근을 α, β, γ라 할 때, (α+β)(β+γ)(γ+α)의 값은?
x>y>0 인 실수 x, y가 x²+y²=10, xy=3을 만족시킬 때, x³−y³의 값은?
이차함수 y=x²−2kx+k²+k−3의 그래프가 직선 y=2x+1에 접할 때, 상수 k의 값은?
−1≤x≤3에서 이차함수 f(x)=x²−2ax+3의 최솟값이 −1이 되도록 하는 모든 실수 a의 값의 합은?
곡선 y=x² 위의 점과 직선 y=2x−5 사이의 거리의 최솟값은?
이차방정식 x²−2ax+a+6=0의 두 근이 모두 1보다 크도록 하는 정수 a의 개수는?
연립부등식 x²−5x+4≤0, x²−(a+2)x+2a<0 을 만족시키는 정수 x가 정확히 2개일 때, 실수 a의 값의 범위는?
items.x: 첫째: 1≤x≤4. 둘째: (x−2)(x−a)<0. a<2이면 정수해는 많아야 1개. a>2이면 2<x<a와 [1,4]의 정수 3,4가 모두 포함되려면 a>4.

items.q: 부등식 |x−1|+|x+3|≤8을 만족시키는 정수 x의 개수는?
모든 실수 x에 대하여 (k−1)x²−2(k−1)x+3>0이 성립하도록 하는 정수 k의 개수는?
1부터 6까지의 자연수 중 서로 다른 세 수를 택해 만들 수 있는 세 자리 자연수 중 3의 배수의 개수는?
items.x: 나머지 0:{3,6}, 1:{1,4}, 2:{2,5}. 합이 3의 배수가 되려면 각 나머지 하나씩: 2³=8가지 조합, 배열 3!=6 → 48.

items.q: 남학생 3명과 여학생 3명이 일렬로 설 때, 여학생끼리는 서로 이웃하지 않고 양 끝 중 적어도 한쪽에는 남학생이 서는 경우의 수는?
items.x: 여학생끼리 이웃 X: 3!·₄P₃=144. 이 중 양 끝이 모두 여학생: 양 끝 틈 2개 고정+가운데 틈 2개 중 1 → 3!·2·3!=72. 144−72=72.

items.q: 정팔각형의 꼭짓점 중 세 개를 이어 만든 삼각형 중에서 정팔각형과 변을 하나도 공유하지 않는 삼각형의 개수는?
x≤y≤z를 만족시키는 음이 아닌 정수 x, y, z에 대하여 방정식 x+y+z=10의 해 (x, y, z)의 개수는?
items.x: 10을 3개 이하의 자연수 합으로 나타내는 분할 수: 1개(1)+2개(5)+3개(8)=14.

items.q: 서로 다른 공 5개를 서로 다른 상자 3개에 빈 상자가 없도록 넣는 경우의 수는?
A=[[1,2],[0,1]]일 때, 행렬 A+A²+A³+…+A¹⁰의 모든 성분의 합은?
A=[[0,1],[2,1]]에 대하여 A⁵=pA+qE (E는 단위행렬)일 때, p+q의 값은?
items.x: A²=A+2E. A³=3A+2E, A⁴=5A+6E, A⁵=5A²+6A=11A+10E → 21.

items.q: 두 점 A(1,2), B(7,−4)에 대하여 선분 AB를 2:1로 내분하는 점을 P, 외분하는 점을 Q라 할 때, 선분 PQ의 길이는?
점 (2,3)을 지나는 직선 중 원점과의 거리가 최대인 직선의 y절편은?
items.x: 원점과 (2,3)을 잇는 선분에 수직인 직선: 2x+3y=13 → y절편 13/3.

items.q: 세 점 A(0,0), B(4,1), C(1,5)를 꼭짓점으로 하는 삼각형 ABC의 넓이를 직선 y=mx가 이등분할 때, m의 값은?
items.x: A를 지나므로 BC의 중점 (5/2, 3)을 지나야 한다. m=3÷(5/2)=6/5.

items.q: 원 x²+y²−4x+6y+k=0이 x축에 접할 때, 상수 k의 값은?
items.x: 중심 (2,−3), 반지름² 13−k. x축에 접 → 반지름 3 → k=4.

items.q: 원 x²+y²=25와 직선 3x+4y=k (k>0)가 만나서 생기는 현의 길이가 8일 때, k의 값은?
점 P(5,0)에서 원 x²+y²=9에 그은 두 접선의 접점을 A, B라 할 때, 삼각형 PAB의 넓이는?
원 (x−3)²+(y−4)²=4 위의 점 P와 두 점 A(−1,0), B(1,0)에 대하여 PA²+PB²의 최솟값은?
items.x: PA²+PB²=2(x²+y²)+2. 원점과 원 위 점의 최소 거리 5−2=3 → 2·9+2=20.

items.q: 두 점 A(−2,0), B(4,0)에 대하여 PA:PB=1:2를 만족시키는 점 P가 그리는 도형의 둘레의 길이는?
원 x²+y²−2x+4y=0을 직선 y=x에 대하여 대칭이동한 후 x축의 방향으로 a만큼 평행이동한 원이 y축에 접할 때, 양수 a의 값은?
두 점 A(1,3), B(4,2)와 y축 위의 점 Q, x축 위의 점 P에 대하여 AQ+QP+PB의 최솟값은?
원 (x−1)²+(y−1)²=1이 x축, y축과 직선 l로 둘러싸인 삼각형(제1사분면)의 내접원이 되도록 직선 l을 그을 때, 이 삼각형의 넓이의 최솟값은?

items.x: 1,2는 포함, 3,4는 제외. 나머지 6개 중 3개 선택: ₆C₃=20.

items.q: 두 조건 p: |x−a|≤2, q: x²−2x−8≤0에 대하여 p가 q이기 위한 충분조건이 되도록 하는 정수 a의 개수는?
양수 x, y에 대하여 (x+1/y)(4y+1/x)의 최솟값은?
x>1일 때, (x²−x+4)/(x−1)의 최솟값은?
f(x)=2x−1, g(x)=x²+1에 대하여 (g∘f)(a)=10을 만족시키는 모든 실수 a의 값의 합은?
f(x)=3x+a에 대하여 f⁻¹(5)=2일 때, (f∘f)⁻¹(8)의 값은?
X={1,2,3,4}에 대하여 X에서 X로의 함수 f가 f∘f=I(항등함수)와 f(1)≠1을 만족시킬 때, 가능한 f의 개수는?
items.x: f는 자기 역함수인 일대일대응. f(1)은 2,3,4 중 하나(3가지), 남은 두 원소는 서로 바꾸거나 고정(2가지) → 6.

items.q: 함수 y=(2x+5)/(x+1)의 그래프가 점 (p,q)에 대하여 대칭이고, 0≤x≤2에서 최댓값 M, 최솟값 m이다. p+q+M+m의 값은?
함수 y=√(x−1)의 그래프와 직선 y=x+k가 서로 다른 두 점에서 만나도록 하는 실수 k의 값의 범위는?
items.x: t=√(x−1)≥0: t²−t+1+k=0이 서로 다른 음이 아닌 두 근 → D=−3−4k>0, 두 근의 곱 1+k≥0 → −1≤k<−3/4 (k=−1이면 t=0,1로 두 점).

items.q: 곡선 y=k/x (k>0)와 직선 y=−x+6이 만나는 두 점을 A, B라 하자. 삼각형 OAB의 넓이가 8일 때, 상수 k의 값은? (O는 원점)
다항식 f(x)를 (x−1)²으로 나눈 나머지는 2x+3이고, x−2로 나눈 나머지는 1이다. f(x)를 (x−1)²(x−2)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(0)의 값은?
0≤x≤2에서 이차함수 f(x)=x²−2ax+2a+3의 최솟값을 g(a)라 할 때, g(a)의 최댓값은?
50 이하의 자연수 n 중에서 {(1+i)/√2}ⁿ + {(1−i)/√2}ⁿ = 0 을 만족시키는 n의 개수는?
items.x: z=(1+i)/√2 → z²=i. n=2m이면 iᵐ+(−i)ᵐ=0 ⇔ m 홀수 ⇔ n≡2 (mod 4). n 홀수면 z와 z̄의 합은 실수부 2배≠0. n=2,6,…,50 → 13개.

items.q: x에 대한 삼차방정식 x³+(k−1)x²+3x−k−3=0이 서로 다른 세 실근을 갖도록 하는 정수 k 중 −10≤k≤10인 것의 개수는?
이차부등식 x²−(a+1)x+a≤0을 만족시키는 정수 x가 정확히 3개가 되도록 하는 모든 정수 a의 값의 합은?
1, 2, 3, 4, 5를 일렬로 나열할 때, 모든 k에 대하여 k번째 자리에 k가 오지 않는 경우의 수는?
X={1,2,3,4}에서 X로의 함수 f 중 f(f(1))=1을 만족시키는 f의 개수는?
원 x²+y²=4 위의 점 P와 두 점 A(4,0), B(0,4)에 대하여 삼각형 PAB의 넓이의 최댓값은?
함수 f(x)=(ax+b)/(x+c)의 그래프가 점 (2,3)에 대하여 대칭이고 점 (0,1)을 지날 때, a+b+c의 값은?
A=[[1,a],[b,1]]이 A²=2A를 만족시키고 a+b=3일 때, 행렬 A¹⁰의 모든 성분의 합은?
a+b=1인 양수 a, b에 대하여 (1+1/a)(1+1/b)의 최솟값은?
직선 y=x 위의 점 P에서 원 (x−4)²+y²=4에 그은 접선의 길이의 최솟값은?
items.x: 접선 길이² = (중심까지 거리)² − r². 최소 거리 4/√2=2√2 → √(8−4)=2.

items.q: A={1,2,3,4,5,6}의 부분집합 중 원소의 합이 홀수인 것의 개수는?
items.x: 홀수 1을 넣고 빼는 쌍을 만들면 합의 홀짝이 바뀐다 → 64의 절반 32.

items.q: U={1,2,…,8}, A={1,2,3,4}, B={3,4,5,6}일 때, X∪A=X∪B를 만족시키는 U의 부분집합 X의 개수는?
items.x: A와 B의 대칭차 {1,2,5,6}은 X에 반드시 포함. 나머지 3,4,7,8은 자유 → 2⁴=16.

items.q: 다항식 P(x)를 x²+x−2로 나눈 나머지는 4x−6이고, x−3으로 나눈 나머지는 16이다. P(x)를 (x²+x−2)(x−3)으로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−x−6으로 나눈 나머지는 2x−4이고, x−1로 나눈 나머지는 −14이다. P(x)를 (x²−x−6)(x−1)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−1)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−3x+2로 나눈 나머지는 5x+5이고, x+1로 나눈 나머지는 −12이다. P(x)를 (x²−3x+2)(x+1)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−x−2로 나눈 나머지는 −3x−5이고, x−4로 나눈 나머지는 23이다. P(x)를 (x²−x−2)(x−4)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(5)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+x−2로 나눈 나머지는 2x+5이고, x로 나눈 나머지는 7이다. P(x)를 (x²+x−2)(x)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(5)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−9로 나눈 나머지는 3x+4이고, x+4로 나눈 나머지는 −29이다. P(x)를 (x²−9)(x+4)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+x−6으로 나눈 나머지는 −3x−4이고, x로 나눈 나머지는 −10이다. P(x)를 (x²+x−6)(x)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(3)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+3x로 나눈 나머지는 2x+3이고, x+1로 나눈 나머지는 7이다. P(x)를 (x²+3x)(x+1)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+5x+6으로 나눈 나머지는 −4x−3이고, x−3으로 나눈 나머지는 −75이다. P(x)를 (x²+5x+6)(x−3)으로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+3x로 나눈 나머지는 −3x+7이고, x−1로 나눈 나머지는 0이다. P(x)를 (x²+3x)(x−1)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−2)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+5x+6으로 나눈 나머지는 −2x−4이고, x+1로 나눈 나머지는 −8이다. P(x)를 (x²+5x+6)(x+1)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−3x+2로 나눈 나머지는 2x+3이고, x−4로 나눈 나머지는 29이다. P(x)를 (x²−3x+2)(x−4)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−1)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−1로 나눈 나머지는 −3x+1이고, x−4로 나눈 나머지는 34이다. P(x)를 (x²−1)(x−4)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−2)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²−2x−3으로 나눈 나머지는 −x−6이고, x로 나눈 나머지는 −18이다. P(x)를 (x²−2x−3)(x)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(−4)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+x−6으로 나눈 나머지는 −4x−5이고, x+2로 나눈 나머지는 11이다. P(x)를 (x²+x−6)(x+2)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(3)의 값은?
다항식 P(x)를 x²+x−6으로 나눈 나머지는 2x−4이고, x−4로 나눈 나머지는 −24이다. P(x)를 (x²+x−6)(x−4)로 나눈 나머지를 R(x)라 할 때, R(3)의 값은?

items.p:
For most of the twentieth century, basketball coaches treated the long two-point shot — taken just inside the three-point line — as a sign of a skilled scorer. Players who could reliably hit that shot were ①ignored, and offenses were often built around them. Then analysts began to do some simple arithmetic. A shot from just inside the line succeeds perhaps 40 percent of the time and is worth two points, so it produces about 0.8 points per attempt. A shot from a step farther back succeeds slightly less often, perhaps 36 percent of the time, but is worth three points, producing about 1.08 points per attempt. The difference looks ②small on a single possession, yet over a season of thousands of shots it can decide a championship.
Once teams accepted this logic, the game changed ③rapidly. The long two nearly disappeared, replaced by shots at the rim and behind the arc. Critics complained that the sport had become ④predictable, with every team running similar plays. Supporters replied that the change simply reflected a better understanding of value. What is striking is not that the numbers were hidden; anyone with a pencil could have calculated them decades earlier. The barrier was _______. Coaches had watched great players make long twos for years, and the vivid memory of those successes made the shot seem more effective than it was. Data did not reveal a new fact so much as it ⑤exposed what habit had kept people from seeing.

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
In 1854, cholera swept through the Soho district of London, killing more than five hundred people in ten days. The dominant theory of the time held that the disease spread through 'miasma,' a poisonous vapor rising from rotting matter. The physician John Snow was ①skeptical. If cholera traveled through the air, he reasoned, it should affect the lungs first; instead, it attacked the digestive system, suggesting that victims had ②inhaled something.
Snow marked each death on a street map and noticed that the cases clustered around a single water pump on Broad Street. He also found telling ③exceptions. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer rather than pump water, were largely spared, while a woman who lived far away but had the Broad Street water delivered to her home because she liked its taste died of the disease. Persuaded by this evidence, local officials removed the pump's handle, and the outbreak, already ④declining, soon ended.
Snow's map is often celebrated as the birth of epidemiology, but its real lesson lies elsewhere. The data alone did not speak; many people could have seen the same deaths and drawn no conclusion. What made Snow's work powerful was that he _______. A pattern on a map becomes evidence only when it is used to test a specific idea. Even so, the miasma theory remained ⑤popular among officials for years, a reminder that good evidence does not always change minds quickly.
o: A Map That Tested a Theory
The Brewery That Caused an Epidemic

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
When a new smartphone is released, many owners of older models suddenly find their devices slow and unsatisfying, even though the phones work exactly as they did the day before. Nothing about the old phone has changed; what has changed is the ①comparison. Psychologists call this effect 'relative deprivation': we judge our possessions not by what they do but by how they measure up against what others have or what is newly available.
This tendency helps explain a puzzling finding. Across many wealthy countries, average incomes have risen ②dramatically over the past half century, yet reported levels of happiness have barely moved. If satisfaction depended on absolute wealth, people today should be far happier than their grandparents. But because each improvement quickly becomes the new ③baseline, gains in comfort are absorbed almost as soon as they arrive.
Marketers understand this perfectly. Advertising rarely tells us that our current possessions are broken; it shows us something slightly better and lets comparison do the rest. The result is a kind of treadmill: we run faster and faster to stay in the same emotional place. Escaping it does not necessarily require ④rejecting material goods. It requires _______ — shifting attention from how our lives rank against others to whether they serve our own purposes. Researchers have found that people who practice gratitude, deliberately noticing what they already have, report ⑤lower life satisfaction than those who do not.
o: Running on the Treadmill of Comparison
Wealth as the Key to Happiness

items.q: [주제] 윗글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Octopuses have about 500 million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog. What makes them remarkable, however, is not only how many neurons they have but where those neurons are. Roughly two-thirds are located not in the central brain but in the eight arms. Each arm can ①taste, touch, and even make simple decisions on its own. An arm that has been separated from the body will still reach for food and attempt to pass it toward where the mouth would be.
This arrangement allows a level of multitasking that would be ②difficult for animals with centralized nervous systems. While the central brain decides on a general goal, such as 'search that crevice for crabs,' the arms work out the details independently, exploring different holes at the same time. The result is a creature that thinks, in a sense, with its whole body.
Scientists studying robotics have taken a strong interest in this design. Traditional robots are controlled by a single processor that must calculate every movement, which makes them ③quick to adapt to unexpected surfaces. Soft robots inspired by octopuses instead give each limb some local control, letting it respond ④immediately to what it touches. Such designs suggest that intelligence need not be _______. It can be distributed, with many small decision-makers cooperating rather than one master controller directing everything. Nature, once again, has ⑤provided a solution that engineers are only beginning to copy.
o: distributed intelligence in octopuses and its inspiration for robots
the diet of octopuses in the deep sea
why dogs are smarter than octopuses

In the 1970s, the city of New York faced a crime problem so severe that some residents avoided the subway altogether. Two researchers later proposed an influential explanation known as the 'broken windows' theory. If a broken window is left ①unrepaired, they argued, it signals that no one cares, inviting further vandalism and, eventually, more serious crime. Small signs of disorder, in other words, can ②discourage larger ones.
The theory led many police departments to crack down on minor offenses such as graffiti and fare evasion. Crime in New York did fall ③sharply in the following decades, and supporters credited the new approach. Yet the evidence is more complicated than the story suggests. Crime also fell in cities that did not adopt the strategy, and many other factors — economic growth, changes in drug markets, an aging population — were operating at the same time. Moreover, aggressive enforcement of minor offenses fell ④unevenly on poor neighborhoods, damaging trust between residents and police.
None of this means that disorder is irrelevant to how people behave. Experiments have shown, for instance, that people are more likely to litter in an alley already covered with trash. The lesson is that _______. A theory can capture a real effect and still be credited with results it did not produce. When several causes operate together, the most memorable explanation is not necessarily the most ⑤accurate.
o: A Real Effect, an Overstated Success
The End of Crime in America
Subways and the Rise of Cities

Before standardized time, every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest overhead, which meant that a town a few dozen kilometers to the west kept a slightly ①different time from its neighbor. For centuries this caused little trouble, because few people traveled fast enough to notice.
The railways changed that. A train leaving one city and arriving in another had to follow a schedule, but whose clock should the schedule use? In the United States at one point, railroads used more than fifty local times, and stations sometimes displayed several clocks side by side. Missed connections and even ②collisions were blamed on the confusion. In 1883, the railroad companies, acting on their own rather than waiting for the government, divided the country into a few time zones.
The decision met with ③resistance. Some people complained that it was unnatural to eat lunch when the sun said it was not yet noon, and newspapers mocked the idea of time controlled by corporations. Yet within a generation, standard time had become so ④familiar that it seemed part of nature itself. The episode shows how _______. A system invented to solve a practical problem for one industry gradually reshaped the daily rhythms of everyone. Today, few people realize that the hour on their phone is the result of a business decision made for trains, and the old solar noon has become almost ⑤relevant to ordinary life.
o: How Trains Set the World's Clocks
The Sun as the Best Clock
A Government Plan for Time Zones

The advice sounds reasonable, but research on bilingual minds suggests that the boundary between languages is far more ①porous than it implies. When bilinguals read a word in one language, related words in their other language are activated automatically, even when the task does not require it. The two vocabularies are not stored in ②shared rooms; they share a single, interconnected house.

On the benefit side, the constant need to select one language and suppress the other appears to train general mental control. Children raised with two languages often perform well on tasks that require ignoring distractions or switching rules.
For learners, the practical lesson is not to ban the first language but to use it ④strategically. Comparing how two languages express the same idea — where they match and where they differ — can deepen understanding of both. items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Many organizations reward employees for meeting numerical targets: sales per month, calls answered per hour, cases closed per week. The logic is straightforward. What gets measured gets managed, and clear numbers make performance easy to ①compare. Yet targets can produce strange behavior. Call-center workers judged on the length of calls may hang up on difficult customers. Teachers evaluated solely on test scores may ②narrow their lessons to what the test covers.
The problem is not that people are dishonest. It is that any number captures only part of what an organization actually values. When the number becomes the goal, effort flows toward the part that is ③ignored and away from the part that is not. The economist Charles Goodhart described this pattern: once a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
This does not mean measurement should be ④abandoned. Without data, managers would rely on impressions, which are often biased. The solution lies in how numbers are used. Some organizations combine several measures so that improving one at the expense of another brings no reward. Others use data mainly for learning — to ask why results differ — rather than for punishment. The wisest approach treats a number as _______. Leaders who forget this may find their organizations ⑤hitting every target while the real work is neglected.
o: When Targets Distort the Work They Measure
How to Answer More Calls per Hour
The End of Measurement in Business

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
When engineers designed the first escalators, they assumed that people would walk up them, using the moving stairs simply to go faster. Instead, most riders stood still. This small observation illustrates a principle that designers now take ①seriously: people use objects in ways their creators did not intend. Paths worn into the grass beside a paved walkway, known as 'desire lines,' reveal where people actually want to go, regardless of where planners have ②placed the sidewalk.
Some universities have turned this principle into a planning method. Instead of paving paths when a new campus opens, they plant grass everywhere and wait. After a year, the routes students have worn into the lawn show the most ③awkward connections between buildings, and those are the routes that get paved. The result is a network that fits real behavior rather than an architect's ④assumptions.
The same idea applies far beyond landscaping. Software companies watch how users click through their programs and redesign features that people avoid. Hospitals study how nurses really move through wards before arranging supply rooms. In each case, the lesson is that _______. Good design begins not with a perfect plan imposed from above but with careful attention to what people already do. Planners who ignore desire lines often find that their carefully laid paths remain ⑤empty while the grass beside them turns to mud.
o: Let People Show You Where the Path Should Go
The Beauty of Green Campus Lawns
Mud: The Enemy of Good Design

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Writing was invented not by poets but by accountants. The earliest known writing, from ancient Mesopotamia about five thousand years ago, consists mostly of records of grain, livestock, and labor. Temple officials needed to keep track of who owed what, and memory alone could not handle the growing ①simplicity of a city economy. Small clay tokens representing goods gradually gave way to marks pressed into clay tablets, and those marks slowly developed into a full system of signs.
For centuries, writing remained a ②specialized tool, mastered by a small class of trained scribes. It took a long time before anyone used it to record stories, laws, or prayers. When they did, the effects were ③profound. A law written on stone could be read by people who had never met the king who issued it. A story copied onto tablets could survive long after the last person who heard it aloud had died.
Some ancient thinkers were ④suspicious of the new technology. In one of Plato's dialogues, Socrates warns that writing will weaken memory, since people will rely on marks outside themselves instead of knowledge within. He was not entirely wrong: oral cultures often display memory feats that seem astonishing today. Yet writing made possible forms of thought that memory alone could not support, such as long arguments that could be examined line by line. Every powerful tool, it seems, _______. The debate Socrates began continues today, as we ask what search engines and AI are doing to our minds, and whether we are ⑤losing skills we no longer practice.
o: From Grain Records to Great Ideas: The Double Edge of Writing

items.q: [주제] 윗글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Volunteers who sign up to help at animal shelters often arrive full of enthusiasm and leave within a few months. Shelter managers have long wondered why. Surveys suggest that the problem is rarely the work itself, which can be dirty and ①tiring. Instead, volunteers drift away when they feel that their effort makes no visible difference or that no one notices what they do.
One shelter tried a simple experiment. Instead of assigning volunteers to random tasks each week, it gave each person responsibility for a small group of animals. Volunteers learned the animals' names, tracked their progress, and were told when 'their' dogs and cats were adopted. Managers also began sending short thank-you notes describing specific contributions. Within a year, the number of volunteers who stayed longer than six months had nearly ②halved.
The change cost almost nothing, yet it addressed two basic human needs: the need to see the ③results of one's work and the need to be recognized by others. Psychologists who study motivation have found the same pattern in workplaces, schools, and sports teams. People will endure ④considerable hardship for a purpose they can see and feel. What drains motivation is not difficulty but _______. Organizations that rely on volunteers, therefore, should spend less effort recruiting new helpers and more effort making existing ones feel that their work ⑤matters.
o: what keeps volunteers motivated over time
the best way to train shelter animals
why animal shelters need more money

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
For decades, nutrition advice was built on studies of single nutrients: fat, sugar, salt, vitamins. Researchers would isolate one component, measure its effects, and issue recommendations. This approach produced real ①successes, such as the discovery that vitamin C prevents scurvy. But it also led to confusing reversals. Eggs were condemned for their cholesterol, then ②rehabilitated. Low-fat products filled supermarket shelves, often with extra sugar added to replace the flavor that fat had provided.
Part of the problem is that people do not eat nutrients; they eat foods, and they eat them in patterns. A nutrient that appears harmful in isolation may behave ③identically inside a whole food, where fiber, water, and other compounds affect how it is absorbed. The sugar in an apple, surrounded by fiber, enters the bloodstream more slowly than the same amount of sugar in a soft drink.
Newer research therefore focuses on overall dietary patterns. Studies of traditional Mediterranean and Japanese diets, for example, suggest that what matters most is not any single ingredient but the ④combination: plenty of vegetables, beans, fish, and minimally processed foods. This shift has a practical advantage. Instead of asking people to track grams of individual nutrients, advice can be expressed in simple terms that anyone can follow. The history of nutrition science reminds us that _______. When we break a system into parts to study it, we must eventually put it back together to understand how it actually works, or our advice will remain ⑤confusing.
o: Beyond Nutrients: Why Whole Diets Matter
The Secret Power of Vitamin C
Low-Fat Foods for a Long Life
Counting Grams of Sugar Every Day

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Imagine two students preparing for the same exam. The first spends three hours on Sunday reviewing all the material at once. The second spends the same total time spread across six short sessions during the week. On the exam, the second student almost always performs ①better, even though both studied for exactly the same amount of time. Psychologists call this the 'spacing effect,' and it is one of the most ②reliable findings in the science of learning, replicated in hundreds of studies over more than a century.
Why does spacing work? One explanation is that forgetting, surprisingly, helps. When we return to material after some time has passed, we must work harder to retrieve it, and this effortful retrieval ③strengthens the memory more than easy repetition does. Cramming feels productive because the information stays fresh in the mind, but that feeling of fluency is ④trustworthy. It reflects short-term familiarity, not durable learning.
Despite the evidence, most students continue to cram. Part of the reason is that the benefits of spacing are delayed, while the comfort of cramming is immediate. Another reason is that school schedules often encourage it, with tests that cover a single unit and are never revisited. Some educators now design courses that deliberately return to earlier topics throughout the year. Their approach reflects a simple principle: _______. Learning that feels slow and slightly difficult in the moment often proves the most ⑤lasting.
o: Why Studying Less at Once Teaches More

Correcting myths is harder than it seems. Simply repeating a myth in order to deny it can strengthen the very association one hopes to break. items.p:
Economists once assumed that people make decisions by carefully weighing costs and benefits. Real behavior, however, is shaped heavily by defaults — the option that takes effect if a person does nothing. In countries where citizens must actively sign up to become organ donors, participation rates are often low. In similar countries where citizens are donors ①automatically unless they choose to opt out, participation is frequently above 90 percent. The values of the two populations are not dramatically ②different; the default is.
Defaults matter for several reasons. Making a choice requires effort, and many people ③rush into decisions that seem complicated or unpleasant. A default also carries an implied recommendation: people assume that whoever set it had good reasons. Finally, switching away from a default can feel like taking ④responsibility for any bad outcome, while staying put feels safer.
Governments and companies have learned to use this power. Retirement plans that enroll workers automatically, while allowing them to leave, have greatly increased savings rates. But the same tool can be used against people's interests, as when subscriptions renew automatically and cancellation is made deliberately difficult. Because defaults shape behavior so strongly, those who design them carry a special obligation. The question is not whether to set a default — some option will always be the default — but _______. A well-chosen default respects people's freedom while making the ⑤beneficial choice the easiest one.
o: The Quiet Power of the Default Option
Why People Refuse to Donate Organs

items.p:

Vegetation also hides the source of the noise; when people cannot see the highway, they think about it less. In addition, trees attract birds and rustle in the wind, adding natural sounds that partly ④amplify the mechanical hum of engines.
These findings matter for city planning. Noise is often treated as a purely physical problem to be solved with engineering. But how people experience their environment depends on more than measurable quantities. A planner who considers only decibels may build an effective wall that residents still dislike, while a planner who considers perception might combine a lower wall with trees and achieve greater satisfaction at lower cost. The broader lesson is that _______. Solutions that ignore the human side of a problem may succeed on paper and still leave people ⑤dissatisfied.

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
When the printing press spread across Europe in the late fifteenth century, it did not immediately produce a flood of new ideas. Most early printed books were religious texts and classical works that had already circulated in handwritten form. Printers, after all, were businesspeople who needed to sell their products, and familiar titles were the ①safest investment. The revolutionary effects of printing emerged only ②instantly, over generations.
One of the most important effects was standardization. When books were copied by hand, every copy contained slightly different errors, and scholars in different cities might be reading ③different versions of the same text. Printing produced thousands of identical copies, allowing readers across Europe to refer to the same page and line. This made it possible to compare observations, point out errors, and build on one another's work with new ④precision. Some historians argue that the scientific revolution depended as much on this shared, stable record as on any individual genius.
The lesson is that the impact of a technology is rarely visible at its birth. Early users tend to apply new tools to old tasks, and the deeper changes come later, as social habits and institutions adapt. Observers who judged printing by its first decades would have concluded that it changed very little. Similarly, we should be cautious about judging today's technologies by their early uses, because _______. The most significant consequences of an invention are often the ones its inventors ⑤never predicted.
o: The Slow Revolution of the Printing Press
A Single Genius Behind Modern Science

items.p:
Basketball players who shoot free throws well in practice sometimes miss badly in the final seconds of a close game. Sports psychologists call this 'choking,' and their research suggests that it often results not from too little attention but from too ①much. A skilled player normally shoots with a smooth, automatic motion controlled by well-practiced routines. Under pressure, however, the player may start ②monitoring each step — the angle of the elbow, the bend of the knees — as if he were a beginner. This conscious control ③improves movements that had become fluent through years of repetition, making them stiff and unreliable.
Several techniques can help. Some players use a fixed pre-shot routine, such as bouncing the ball exactly three times, which keeps attention on a familiar sequence rather than on individual muscles. Others focus on an external target, like the front of the rim, instead of on their own body. Practicing under simulated pressure, with spectators or consequences, can also make high-stakes situations feel more ④ordinary.
The phenomenon is not limited to sports. Musicians, public speakers, and students taking important exams report similar experiences. In each case, the lesson is that _______. Once a skill has been mastered, trusting it may be more effective than trying to control it. The harder people try to guarantee a perfect performance by watching themselves closely, the more likely they are to ⑤disrupt the very process that makes performance possible.
o: Thinking Too Hard: Why Experts Choke Under Pressure
How to Win Every Close Game
The Physics of a Perfect Free Throw

items.p:
Many online services are free to use, but economists warn that 'free' is misleading. When you do not pay for a product with money, you often pay with something else: your attention and your data. Social media platforms earn revenue by selling advertisers access to their users, which means that the platform's real customers are the advertisers, while the users are closer to the ①product being sold.
This business model creates a particular incentive. The longer users stay, the more advertisements they see, so platforms are ②designed to capture as much time as possible. Features such as endless scrolling, autoplay, and personalized notifications are not ③accidental conveniences; they are carefully tested tools for increasing engagement. Engagement, in turn, tends to be highest for content that provokes strong emotions, including outrage, which may help explain why online discussions so often become ④polarized.
None of this means that users are helpless or that free services provide no value. Many people benefit greatly from staying in touch with friends or finding information quickly. But understanding the economic logic behind a service changes how we might use it. A person who knows that a feed has been arranged to keep him scrolling can make more deliberate choices about when to stop. Recognizing that _______ is the first step toward taking back some control. In the attention economy, the most ⑤abundant resource is not information but our limited capacity to focus.
o: Paying with Attention: The Hidden Price of Free Apps
How to Earn Money from Social Media

items.p:
In earthquake-prone regions, engineers have learned that the strongest building is not always the most rigid one. A completely stiff structure transfers the full force of the ground's shaking to its upper floors, which can cause walls to crack and collapse. Modern designs therefore allow buildings to ①move in controlled ways. Some skyscrapers rest on base isolators — layers of rubber and steel that let the ground shift beneath the building while the structure above moves much ②more.
Other buildings use enormous weights called tuned mass dampers. Placed near the top, a damper swings in the ③opposite direction to the building's sway, absorbing energy and reducing movement. Taipei 101, once the tallest building in the world, contains a steel ball weighing more than 600 tons that visitors can see from an observation deck.
These ideas have roots in traditional architecture. Wooden pagodas in Japan have survived centuries of earthquakes partly because their floors are loosely connected around a central pillar, allowing each level to sway ④independently. Engineers studying these structures found that flexibility, not strength alone, explained their survival. The principle applies beyond buildings: systems that can _______ often outlast those that try to resist every force head-on. A tree that bends in a storm, after all, is more likely to survive than one that stands ⑤rigid against the wind.
o: flexibility as a key to earthquake-resistant design
why pagodas are made of stone

items.p:
Patients with severe memory loss caused by Alzheimer's disease sometimes cannot recognize their own children, yet they can sing every word of songs they learned decades earlier. Researchers have documented this pattern many times, and it suggests that musical memory is stored and retrieved somewhat ①differently from memory for facts and events. Brain imaging studies indicate that some regions involved in musical memory are among the ②last to be damaged by the disease.
Care homes have begun to use this insight. Programs that create personalized playlists of music from each resident's youth report striking effects: residents who rarely speak may begin to ③sing, move to the rhythm, or talk about memories the songs bring back. Staff members describe moments in which a person seems to ④disappear for the length of a song. Although music cannot reverse the disease, it can improve mood, reduce anxiety, and make daily care easier.
The findings also raise broader questions about memory. We often think of the self as a collection of facts we can state — names, dates, places. But music suggests that identity is also stored in feelings, rhythms, and bodily habits that may outlast explicit knowledge. In this view, _______. A person who has forgotten the year she married may still remember how the first dance felt. Caregivers who understand this may find ways to reach patients that ⑤ordinary conversation cannot.
o: The Songs That Remain When Memories Fade
Why Patients Should Avoid Old Songs

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
When a honeybee colony grows too large, about half of its members leave with the old queen to find a new home. The swarm settles temporarily on a tree branch while a few hundred scout bees search the surrounding area for suitable cavities. What happens next is a remarkable example of collective decision-making. No single bee ①compares all the options. Instead, each scout that finds a promising site returns and performs a dance to advertise it, dancing more ②vigorously for better sites.
Other scouts are recruited by these dances, visit the advertised sites, and, if they agree, begin dancing for them too. Support for weaker sites gradually ③fades, because scouts naturally stop dancing after a while and poor sites attract fewer new supporters. Eventually, when enough scouts gather at one site — a kind of quorum — the swarm lifts off and flies there. Studies show that swarms ④rarely choose the best available site, even though no individual has evaluated every option.
Biologists see in this process lessons for human groups. The bees avoid two common traps: deciding too quickly based on the first acceptable option, and being dominated by a single powerful voice. Information comes from many independent explorers, and enthusiasm must be earned through the quality of the site. Human committees, by contrast, often let the most senior or confident member steer the discussion. The bees suggest that _______. A good decision may emerge most reliably when no one is in charge, provided that each voice reports honestly and ⑤independently.
o: Swarm Wisdom: How Bees Choose a Home Without a Leader
Trees as Permanent Homes for Swarms

items.q: [주제] 윗글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
The placebo effect is well known: patients who receive an inactive pill often feel better because they expect to. Less familiar is its dark twin, the nocebo effect. When people expect a treatment to cause harm, they frequently ①experience the side effects they were warned about, even if the treatment contains no active ingredient. In some clinical trials, a substantial share of participants taking sugar pills ②stopped because of side effects such as headaches or nausea.
The nocebo effect creates a difficult problem for doctors. Patients have a right to know about possible side effects, and ethical medicine requires honest information. Yet the very act of listing those effects may ③increase the chance that patients will experience them. A patient told that a drug 'often causes dizziness' may notice ordinary moments of lightheadedness and attribute them to the medicine.
Researchers have explored ways to inform patients without frightening them. One approach is framing: saying that '90 percent of patients experience no side effects' rather than 'one in ten patients experiences side effects,' even though the two statements mean the same thing. Another is explaining that many reported symptoms occur just as often in people taking placebos. The goal is not to hide the truth but to present it so that it does not become ④self-fulfilling. The nocebo effect reminds us that _______. Words spoken in a doctor's office can act on the body almost as ⑤weakly as the medicine itself.

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
On a hot summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This 'urban heat island' arises because asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb sunlight and ①release it slowly as heat, while the lack of trees reduces shade and the cooling effect of evaporation. As heat waves become more frequent, the problem is no longer a mere ②inconvenience; it is a serious health risk, especially for elderly people living without air conditioning.
One surprisingly simple solution is to change the color of roofs. A white or reflective roof can bounce back much of the sunlight that a dark roof would absorb, lowering the roof's surface temperature by tens of degrees. Cities such as New York have organized volunteers to paint thousands of rooftops white. Studies suggest that widespread use of cool roofs could ③raise peak summer temperatures across a city and cut energy use for air conditioning.
Other strategies include planting street trees, creating green roofs covered with vegetation, and using lighter-colored pavement. Each has costs and limitations. Trees take years to grow and require maintenance, while reflective surfaces can create glare. Yet together these measures show that _______. Because the poorest neighborhoods often have the fewest trees and the most pavement, cooling strategies can also reduce ④inequality. A city's temperature, it turns out, is partly a ⑤design choice.
o: Cooling the City: Design Against the Heat Island
Why Countryside Is Hotter Than Cities

When students are asked to judge whether a website is trustworthy, most do what they were taught in school: they read the page carefully, check whether it looks professional, and examine its 'About' section. Polished websites created by advocacy groups or companies can look just as credible as those of independent experts, and a well-written 'About' page tells you only what the site wants you to believe.

items.q: [주제] 윗글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that nearly half may disappear by the end of this century. Most endangered languages have only a few thousand speakers, and many are spoken mainly by elderly people. When children grow up speaking a more widely used language at school and online, the older language can ①vanish within a single generation.
Why should the loss of a language matter to people who never spoke it? One reason is scientific. Each language represents a unique way of organizing experience, and studying the full range of human languages helps researchers understand what is ②universal about the human mind and what is shaped by culture. Some languages, for example, describe directions using north and south rather than left and right, and their speakers show ③remarkable skill at keeping track of orientation.
Another reason concerns knowledge. Languages often contain detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals, and environmental conditions, built up over centuries of close observation. When the language disappears, much of this knowledge may ④disappear with it. Communities around the world are now working to revive their languages through recordings, dictionaries, and classes for children. Their efforts reflect a belief that _______. A language, in this sense, is not just a tool for communication but a record of how a people has understood the world, and its loss is ⑤easy to reverse.
o: why the disappearance of languages matters
how to learn a new language quickly
the most widely spoken language in the world

items.p:
In the famous 'marshmallow test' of the 1960s and 1970s, young children were offered a choice: eat one marshmallow now, or wait alone for several minutes and receive two. Children who waited longer were later found, on average, to have better school results. The study was widely interpreted as showing that self-control is a ①flexible personal trait that predicts success in life.
Later researchers questioned this interpretation. In one variation, children first experienced an adult who either kept or ②broke a promise to bring better art supplies. Children who had dealt with the unreliable adult waited far less time for the second marshmallow. Their choice was not necessarily a failure of willpower; it was a ③reasonable response to an environment in which promises were not kept. If you have learned that rewards often fail to arrive, taking what is available now makes sense.
Larger follow-up studies also found that the link between waiting and later achievement became much ④weaker once family income and home environment were taken into account. Children from more stable, wealthier homes tended both to wait longer and to do better in school, partly because their worlds had taught them that waiting pays off. The lesson is that _______. Behavior that looks like a lack of self-control may sometimes be a sensible adaptation to uncertainty, and improving children's ⑤circumstances may matter as much as training their willpower.
o: Waiting for a Reward Depends on Trusting It Will Come

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Basketball fans have long believed in the 'hot hand': the idea that a player who has made several shots in a row is more likely to make the next one. In 1985, a group of psychologists analyzed shooting records and concluded that the hot hand was an ①illusion. Streaks, they argued, appeared no more often than chance would predict, and fans were simply seeing patterns in random sequences. For decades, the study was cited as a classic example of how the human mind ②finds order where none exists.
In 2015, however, two economists pointed out a subtle statistical error in the original analysis. When you look at short sequences and ask how often a hit follows a series of hits, the expected rate under pure chance is actually ③lower than the overall shooting percentage, not equal to it. Once this bias was corrected, the original data showed evidence of a modest hot hand after all.
The story carries a double lesson. First, people do sometimes see patterns that are not there, and skepticism toward our intuitions is healthy. Second, the experts who correct popular beliefs can also make mistakes, and their conclusions deserve the same ④careless scrutiny. Neither the fans nor the original researchers were entirely right. Science, in this case, did not deliver a final verdict but showed that _______. The best response to a confident claim, whether from a fan or a professor, is to ask how it was ⑤tested.
o: The Hot Hand Returns: When Experts Are Corrected
Why Basketball Fans Are Always Wrong
How to Become a Hot Shooter

Only a small fraction of the plastic ever produced has actually been recycled. In many offices, open-plan layouts replaced private rooms with the promise that removing walls would ①discourage collaboration. Managers imagined employees casually exchanging ideas across shared desks. When researchers actually measured behavior, however, they found the opposite. After two companies moved to open offices, face-to-face interaction dropped by roughly 70 percent, while email and messaging ②increased.
Why would removing walls reduce conversation? One explanation is that people in open spaces feel ③exposed. Knowing that colleagues can hear every word and see every screen, employees create privacy in other ways: they put on headphones, avoid eye contact, and move discussions online, where they can control who is listening. The open office, designed to bring people together, ended up teaching them to ④withdraw.
This does not mean that physical layout is unimportant. Spaces strongly shape behavior, but rarely in simple ways. Designers who assume that people will act as intended often overlook how humans adapt to protect their needs, such as the need for privacy and concentration. Some companies now offer a mix of spaces: quiet rooms for focused work, small meeting areas, and shared zones for casual contact. Such designs reflect the idea that _______. A workplace that respects both concentration and connection may produce more genuine collaboration than one that simply ⑤forces people into the same room.
o: Fewer Walls, Less Talk: The Open-Office Paradox

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Most people assume that adding more lanes, more options, or more information always improves a system. A surprising counterexample comes from traffic engineering. In 1968, a mathematician named Dietrich Braess showed that adding a new road to a network can sometimes make travel ①slower for everyone. The reason lies in individual choice. Each driver picks the route that seems fastest for himself, but when everyone does the same, the new road becomes ②crowded and pushes traffic onto other roads in a way that raises the average travel time.
This result, known as Braess's paradox, is not merely theoretical. When the city of Seoul removed an elevated highway in 2003 to restore the Cheonggyecheon stream, many predicted traffic chaos. Instead, traffic in the area did not get significantly worse, and in some respects it ③worsened, as drivers adjusted their routes and some switched to public transport. Similar cases have been reported in other cities.
The paradox reveals a broader truth about complex systems. Because the behavior of the whole emerges from many individual decisions, improving one part does not ④automatically improve the system. Engineers must think about how people will respond to a change, not only about the change itself. The paradox also suggests that _______. In a network of interacting choices, less can sometimes be more, and removing an option may lead to ⑤better outcomes for all.
o: When More Roads Mean Slower Traffic
The Fastest Route in Every City

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Scientists once believed that the adult human brain could not grow new neurons and that its structure was largely ①flexible after childhood. Over the past few decades, this view has been overturned. Research has shown that the brain continually ②reorganizes itself in response to experience, a property known as neuroplasticity. London taxi drivers, who must memorize thousands of streets, develop a larger hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, than people in other jobs.
Neuroplasticity works in both directions. Skills that are practiced become stronger, while those that are ③neglected tend to weaken, as the brain reallocates resources. Musicians who stop practicing lose some of their finger dexterity, and people who rely heavily on GPS may show reduced activity in brain regions used for navigation. In this sense, the brain is ④shaped by what we repeatedly do.
This discovery carries both hope and responsibility. On the hopeful side, people recovering from strokes can sometimes regain lost abilities through intensive training, as healthy parts of the brain take over damaged functions. On the responsible side, our daily habits are constantly sculpting the organ that makes us who we are. The question is not whether our brains will change but _______. Choosing what to practice, it turns out, is also choosing who we ⑤become.
o: You Become What You Practice: The Changing Brain
The Brain Stops Growing at Twenty

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
When a company launches a product that turns out to be harmful, executives often say that no one could have foreseen the problem. Sometimes this is true. But in many cases, warnings existed and were ①ignored. Engineers raised concerns that never reached decision-makers, or decision-makers heard the concerns and chose to proceed anyway. Researchers who study such failures have identified a common pattern: organizations ②punish bad news.
In such organizations, employees learn that reporting a problem brings blame rather than thanks. The rational response is to stay quiet, ③soften warnings, or wait for someone else to speak. Over time, leaders receive an increasingly ④accurate picture of reality, filtered through layers of people trying to avoid trouble. By the time a problem becomes impossible to hide, it may also be impossible to fix cheaply.
Some industries have deliberately designed systems to counter this tendency. In aviation, pilots and crew are encouraged to report errors and near misses, and reports are often protected from punishment. The goal is to learn from small mistakes before they become disasters. Hospitals have begun adopting similar practices. These efforts reflect the insight that _______. An organization's safety depends less on whether mistakes happen — they always will — than on whether people feel ⑤safe talking about them.
o: Why Organizations Need to Welcome Bad News

items.p:
Every year, millions of people make New Year's resolutions, and most abandon them within a few weeks. Psychologists who study habit formation suggest that the problem is often not a lack of motivation but a reliance on it. Motivation is ①strong at the start of a new plan but rises and falls with mood, energy, and circumstance. A habit, by contrast, runs ②automatically once it is established, triggered by cues in the environment rather than by a fresh decision each day.
For this reason, experts recommend designing the environment instead of relying on willpower. Someone who wants to read more might leave a book on the pillow; someone who wants to eat less sugar might simply stop buying sweets. Making a desired behavior easy and an undesired one ③convenient shifts the balance without requiring constant effort. Small starting goals also help. A person who commits to one push-up a day is more likely to build a lasting routine than one who promises an hour at the gym, because the small action is ④easy to repeat even on bad days.
Over time, repeated actions can change how people see themselves. Someone who exercises regularly may begin to think, 'I am the kind of person who exercises,' and this identity then supports the habit further. The lesson is that _______. Lasting change depends less on bursts of determination than on ⑤systems that make good choices the natural default.
o: Design Your Habits, Don't Rely on Willpower
One Hour at the Gym Every Day

This approach reflects the belief that _______. A history that listens only to those who could write tells us mainly about the ⑤majority.
o: Recovering the Voices History Left Out
Why Kings Wrote the Best Diaries

items.q: [주제] 윗글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
The idea that we use only ten percent of our brains is one of the most ①accurate myths in popular culture. It appears in films, advertisements, and self-help books promising to unlock hidden potential. Neuroscientists, however, find no support for it. Brain imaging shows that over the course of a day, virtually all regions of the brain are ②active, even during sleep. Damage to almost any area, however small, produces some loss of function.
The brain is also an expensive organ. Although it makes up only about two percent of body weight, it ③consumes roughly twenty percent of the body's energy. From an evolutionary perspective, it would make little sense for such a costly organ to leave ninety percent of its capacity unused. Natural selection tends to ④eliminate wasteful structures over time.
Why, then, does the myth persist? Part of its appeal lies in its promise. If most of our brain is unused, then we might become dramatically smarter with the right technique or product. The myth flatters our hopes while offering an easy explanation for why we have not yet achieved them. Recognizing it as false need not be discouraging. The real lesson of neuroscience is that _______. Improvement comes not from awakening sleeping regions but from ⑤training the brain we already use fully.
o: why the ten-percent brain myth is false and why it persists
how to unlock hidden brain power with products
the brain's energy use during sleep only

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter, a spacecraft worth more than 100 million dollars. The cause was not a dramatic mechanical failure but a simple ①mismatch of units. One engineering team calculated thrust in pounds, while another team's software expected newtons. The numbers passed between the teams without ②conversion, and the spacecraft approached Mars at the wrong altitude and was destroyed.
What makes the case instructive is that the error was ③easy to detect. Small discrepancies in the spacecraft's path had appeared during the months-long journey, and some engineers noticed them. But the concerns were not pursued with enough urgency, partly because procedures for raising such issues were unclear and partly because the mission was under pressure to stay on schedule. The mistake itself was trivial; the system that allowed it to ④survive was not.
Investigators concluded that the deeper problem lay in communication and verification. Complex projects involve many teams, each making assumptions that others may not share. When those assumptions are never stated explicitly, errors can slip through the gaps between groups. The lesson applies far beyond space exploration: _______. A single missing label on a number cost more than 100 million dollars, a reminder that small details can have ⑤trivial consequences when no one is responsible for checking them.
o: Lost in Translation: How a Unit Error Destroyed a Spacecraft
The Mechanical Failure of a Rocket
Why Mars Is Impossible to Reach

items.q: [제목] 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p:
Many people believe that creative ideas arrive suddenly, in a flash of inspiration. Stories of inventors shouting 'Eureka!' in the bath support this image. Yet studies of creative work tell a different story. Most breakthroughs come after long periods of ①preparation, during which a person gathers knowledge, struggles with a problem, and tries many approaches that fail. The sudden insight, when it comes, is usually the final step of a long process rather than a ②gift from nowhere.
Researchers have also found that stepping away from a problem can help. After intense effort, taking a walk, sleeping, or working on something unrelated often allows the mind to make ③connections it could not make under pressure. This period, sometimes called incubation, works only because of the effort that came before it. Someone who has not wrestled with a problem has nothing to ④forget.
These findings have practical implications for students and workers. Creativity cannot be scheduled, but it can be prepared for. Filling the mind with diverse knowledge, working hard on difficult problems, and then allowing time for rest creates the conditions in which insight is more likely. The romantic image of the lone genius waiting for inspiration may be appealing, but it hides the truth that _______. Inspiration, in other words, tends to visit those who have already done the ⑤work.
o: Rest Is the Enemy of Creativity

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: Experts often make poor teachers, not because they lack knowledge but because they have too much of it in a form they can no longer inspect. Once a skill becomes automatic, the intermediate steps that a beginner must consciously assemble collapse into a single, effortless act. The chess master does not 'see' that a knight is undefended; she simply perceives a weak position. Asked to explain, she reconstructs a chain of reasoning that may bear little resemblance to what actually happened in her mind. The irony is that the very process that produced mastery has _______, leaving the expert with a fluent performance but an unreliable account of how that performance is achieved.
o: erased the traces of its own construction
made the expert more aware of each step
left beginners unable to imitate experts
depended on explicit rules from the start
encouraged experts to teach more often
items.x: 자동화된 숙련은 중간 단계를 하나로 압축해 버려, 전문가는 자신이 어떻게 하는지 설명하지 못한다 → '자신이 만들어진 흔적을 지워버렸다'.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: We tend to assume that a map is valuable in proportion to its detail. Yet a map drawn at a scale of one to one, showing every pebble and blade of grass, would be useless: it would be as large and as bewildering as the territory itself. A map earns its usefulness precisely through what it leaves out. The subway map that distorts distances and straightens curves is far more helpful to a commuter than an accurate satellite image. The same holds for scientific models, which deliberately ignore friction, air resistance, or individual variation. Their power lies not in mirroring reality but in _______.
o: selectively discarding what does not serve a purpose
capturing every possible variable at once
being as large as what they represent
items.x: 지도와 모델은 생략을 통해 유용해진다 → '목적에 맞지 않는 것을 선택적으로 버리는 것'.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: When a company offers customers twenty flavors of jam instead of six, more people stop to look, but fewer actually buy. Each additional option adds not only another possibility but another opportunity for regret. A shopper who picks one jar from twenty must live with the nagging thought that one of the other nineteen might have been better. In this sense, abundance of choice can function less as freedom than as _______.
items.x: 선택지가 많을수록 후회의 가능성이 커져 구매(결정)를 덜 하게 된다 → '결정을 방해하는 짐'.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: Historians of technology have noted that the arrival of a new medium rarely destroys the old one outright. Instead, the older medium is pushed to discover what it can do that the newcomer cannot. Painting, freed by photography from the duty of faithful representation, turned toward impression, abstraction, and the depiction of inner states. Radio, once television took over the evening hours, reinvented itself around the commute and the kitchen. What looks at first like replacement is more often _______.
o: a victory of the cheaper medium
an accident with no lasting effect
items.x: 새 매체가 등장하면 기존 매체는 사라지지 않고 고유한 역할을 재발견한다 → '강요된 목적의 재정의'.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: In team sports, statistics usually reward the player who scores. But coaches know that some of the most valuable contributions never appear in a box score: the defender who forces an opponent into a bad shot, the teammate who sets a screen that frees the shooter. A team built only from players with impressive individual numbers often underperforms, because those numbers can be inflated by _______.
o: work that other teammates quietly did
the size of the home crowd
rules that favor the visiting team
items.x: 득점 기록은 스크린·수비 등 보이지 않는 동료의 기여로 부풀려질 수 있다.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: A rule that is never broken tells us little about whether it is necessary. If a town has never had a flood, residents may conclude that the expensive levee was a waste of money, when in fact the levee is the reason there has been no flood. Successful prevention is, by its nature, invisible: its evidence is an event that did not happen. This creates a peculiar political problem, since those who invest in prevention _______.
o: can rarely point to proof that their investment worked
are always praised when disasters occur elsewhere
usually spend less than those who respond to crises
tend to exaggerate the danger of floods
receive credit as soon as the project is finished
items.x: 예방의 성공은 '일어나지 않은 일'이라 증명이 어렵다 → 투자 효과를 입증할 증거를 제시하기 어렵다.

items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.p: Language learners often believe that they must understand every word before they can understand a sentence. Skilled readers do the opposite. They form a rough hypothesis about the meaning of a passage from context, then use individual words to confirm or revise it. Comprehension, in other words, moves _______ as much as it builds upward from the parts.
